Micromobility & Urban Infrastructure

SolvingThe Last Mile

How Taiwan's world class bike-share network solved the last mile, and where it still falls short.

YouBike, My Love

What I was most impressed with in Taiwan was its micromobility. Since I did not have access to a scooter or a car, much of my travels struggled with the last "mile." However, their bike-share system, YouBike, saved me more times than I could count due to its availability, ease, and affordability.

Across the island, the YouBike network has grown to over 8,800 stations and nearly 80,000 bikes, including over 3,500 stations in the Greater Taipei Area alone. A remarkable innovation was the transition to YouBike 2.0 — a technological leap that moved the "brain" of the system from the stationary dock to the bike itself. This allows for slim, solar-powered poles that require no complex electrical wiring, enabling the city to tuck stations into narrow alleyways and residential corners where the older 1.0 docks could never fit.

They have also introduced the 2.0E e-bike, which provides pedal assist boost up to 25 km/h (though I have personally hit 50 km/h on downhills haha) making longer commutes and uphills effortless, with a battery-maintenance fee of NT$20 per half-hour.

Additionally, with availability information built directly into Google Maps and their app, the system simplifies the user experience when searching for transit options. YouBike integrates directly with EasyCard, iPASS, and the TPASS monthly commuter program, meaning instead of subscribing to yet another app, riders simply tap on and off. This low barrier of entry is a stark contrast to the bike-share systems in Hamilton and Toronto, which require dedicated app subscriptions.

The cherry on top is that in many districts, the first 30 minutes remain free, rooted in a "Green Transport" initiative to reduce scooter congestion and carbon emissions. A student can grab a bike to get to class, or an office worker can attend a cross-district meeting, often without spending a single dollar.

Infrastructure in Cities: Excellence and Fragmentation

While I have sung praises about Taiwanese bike-share infrastructure and density, there is a noticeable weak point across multiple cities: bicycle infrastructure. The intra-connectivity was fantastic, with wide bike lanes threading through the city and the best harbour trail I have ever experienced — one I rode daily during my Chinese New Year break. But the inter-connectivity, the links between paths, was extremely lacking.

To access the harbour path, I would have to push my bike up a bridge, execute a U-turn, reach the other side, and arrive at a stairwell with no ramp and no alternative access point. Google Maps would suggest a route that simply did not exist when I arrived. Other bridge pathways would abruptly lead to dead ends or inaccessible stairways. This fragmentation extends to sidewalks too: often in the side streets outside the main arterial paths, there is no municipally built pavement — only disjointed sections forced together, making accessibility a challenge for anyone without a fully able body.

Suggested Google Maps route requring crossing a highway

A bridge crossing that leads to a dead end for cyclists

Network continuity is a more significant predictor of cycling uptake than any individual infrastructure quality metric. A high-quality trail requiring an inaccessible transition is, for many users, functionally unreachable.

Buehler & Pucher, 2012 — City Cycling, MIT Press

What I experienced maps closely onto what transportation scholars call the "missing link" problem in cycling network design. Elevated road infrastructure creates what planners call vertical discontinuity which is a break in the cycling surface that cannot be resolved without climbing stairs or sharing car lanes. In Copenhagen and Amsterdam, this was addressed through dedicated cycle ramps integrated into bridge structures from the outset. Taiwan's rapid trail expansion appears to have outpaced the resolution of these transition points, producing exactly the kind of infrastructure designed without considering the desire lines of non-motorized users.

The Institutional Patchwork

The fundamental challenge facing Taiwan's cycling ambitions is institutional fragmentation. While the island boasts world-class primary trails, these routes usually fall under the strict mandates of river basin authorities and tourism bureaus which have the funding and focus to maintain high standards. The breakdown occurs in the "connective tissue": the streets and passages that link scenic routes to where people actually live and work. This space is a jurisdictional patchwork quilt, overseen by road bureaus, district offices, and private landlords, each with competing priorities like scooter parking or traffic throughput.

As urban planners Pucher and Buehler pointed out in their landmark 2008 study, this lack of cross-jurisdictional coordination is the "Achilles heel" of urban cycling. Their research into Dutch and Danish success stories suggests that while municipal initiatives are valuable, they are functionally incomplete without multi-level governance to bridge the gaps. Between 2008 and 2022, the Taiwanese government expanded the cycling network from 900 km to over 4,000 km, anchored by the iconic 960.8 km Cycling Route No. 1.

The issue is that since the system feels so close to being world-class, the sudden disruption of these paths becomes amplified. The next step for Taiwan to reach the next level is to bridge said gaps (literally and institutionally)to ensure a smooth journey for those unwilling to scale a bridge and execute a U-turn in the dark.
